issues.legal_issue: An ancestral impartible estate does not become the separate property of its current holder merely because it is impartible, and its joint-family character continues unless junior members renounce their right of succession.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that the family estate was impartible and that succession followed lineal primogeniture, making him entitled to exclusive possession as the current office-holder.

The lower courts found that the alleged custom of impartibility and primogeniture had not been proved; the legal argument before the Supreme Court proceeded on the assumption that the estate was impartible.
The claimant and the other parties descended from a common family ancestor.
issues.conclusion: Even if an ancestral estate is impartible, impartibility alone does not make it the separate property of the holder or destroy the right of survivorship. The family ceases to be joint in respect of the estate only if the junior members expressly or impliedly renounce their succession rights.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, custom may displace some ordinary incidents of joint-family property in an impartible estate, but survivorship remains unless renounced. The Court relied principally on Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, Baijnath Prasad Singh v. Tej Bali Singh, Collector of Gorakhpur v. Ram Sunder Mal, Anant Bhikappa Patil v. Shankar Ramchandra Patil, and Chinnathayi v. Kulasekara Pandiya Naicker; it distinguished Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj Manne Sultan Bahadur and Rajah Velugoti Kumara Krishna Yachendra Varu because those cases concerned different statutory schemes and facts.

rule.if: ancestral_family_estate and impartible_estate and not junior_members_renounced_succession

predicates.ancestral_family_estate: The estate descended within a family as ancestral property.
predicates.impartible_estate: The estate could not be divided under a custom or other rule governing its tenure or succession.
predicates.junior_members_renounced_succession: The junior members expressly or impliedly gave up their right to succeed to the estate.

issues.definition: When an ancestral estate is impartible and the junior members have not renounced succession, the estate retains its joint-family character and the right of survivorship.

issues.legal_issue: Abolition of a watan and regrant of its land to the holder for the time being extinguish watan-specific incidents but do not extinguish the family’s other rights under personal law.
material_facts: The family estate included lands held as watan property.
The claimant was recognized as the watandar after his father’s death and the lands were regranted to him as occupant after the statutory abolition and resumption.
The other family members claimed interests in the properties as members of the joint family.
issues.conclusion: The abolition and regrant changed the tenure and character of the land as watan property and extinguished incidents attached to the watan, including impartibility and primogeniture insofar as they were such incidents. They did not extinguish other rights under personal law. If the watan land was joint-family property, its regrant to the holder for the time being enured to the benefit of the entire joint family.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4(1) of the Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans Abolition Act, 1950, and sections 4 and 7 of the Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, abolish the watan, resume the land, and provide for regrant. They alter the tenure but do not abrogate personal-law rights unrelated to the watan tenure. The Court relied on Collector of South Satara v. Laxman Mahadev Deshpande and approved the reasoning in Laxmibai Sadashiv Date v. Ganesh Shankar Date and Dhondi Vithoba Koli v. Mahadeo Dagdu Koli.

predicates.watan_land_was_joint_family_property: Members of a family held the land as joint-family property before its watan tenure ended.
predicates.watan_land_was_resumed: The land was taken back under a measure abolishing the watan tenure.
predicates.watan_land_was_regranted_to_current_hold: The land was granted again as occupancy land to the person who held the watan at the relevant time.

issues.definition: When joint-family watan land is resumed and regranted to its current holder, the regrant benefits the family and does not by itself extinguish the family’s other personal-law rights.

issues.legal_issue: A person with a hereditary interest in watan property may qualify as a watandar even without holding the hereditary office or performing its attached services.
material_facts: The claimant held the hereditary office and received the regrant, while other family members asserted interests in the watan property.
The Court considered whether the statutory meaning of watandar was limited to a person who held both the hereditary office and an interest in the property.
issues.conclusion: The definition of watandar includes a person who has a hereditary interest in watan property even if that person does not hold the hereditary office or perform its attached services; the relevant family members could therefore be treated as watandars of the same watan for the statutory scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, is to be read as one definition, with its inclusive portion supplementing the primary meaning. The Court followed the Full Bench ruling in Vijayasingrao Balasaheb Shinde Desai v. Janardanrao Narayanrao Shinde Desai and the approach in Kadappo Bapurao Desai v. Krishtappa Bachappa Desai; it overruled Tarabai Sriniwas Naik Guttal v. Murtacharya Anantacharya.

predicates.person_has_hereditary_interest_in_watan_: A person has a hereditary interest in property held as part of a watan.
predicates.person_belongs_to_watan_family: The person belongs to the family associated with that watan.
predicates.person_does_not_hold_hereditary_office: The person does not hold the hereditary office associated with the watan.

issues.definition: A family member with a hereditary interest in watan property may qualify as a watandar even without holding the associated hereditary office.

issues.legal_issue: Commutation of the services attached to a watan does not, by itself, convert watan land into the watandar’s private property.
material_facts: Service attached to the hereditary office had been commuted in return for a quit-rent on the land.
The office had not thereby been abolished, and the land remained associated with the hereditary office before the later statutory abolition.
issues.conclusion: Commutation relieved the watandars from performing services but did not convert the land into their private property or make it freely alienable; while the office survived, the land retained its character as watan property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles concerning service commutation under the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, and relied on Collector of South Satara v. Laxman Mahadev Deshpande, which approved the relevant reasoning in Appaji Bapuji v. Keshav Shamrav. It also referred to Bachharam Datta Patil v. Vishwanath Pundalik Patil concerning the State’s power to abolish or resume a watan.

predicates.watan_services_were_commuted: The holder was relieved from performing the services attached to the watan in return for a payment or quit-rent.
predicates.hereditary_office_survived: The hereditary office was not abolished when the services were commuted.

issues.definition: If services are commuted while the hereditary office survives, the land remains attached to the watan rather than becoming the holder’s private property.

issues.legal_issue: Restrictions requiring official sanction and payment before transfer or partition do not create an absolute statutory bar to transfer or partition once those conditions are met.
material_facts: The land had been regranted as occupancy land.
The applicable provisions restricted transfer or partition by metes and bounds unless prior sanction was obtained and the prescribed amount was paid.
issues.conclusion: The restrictions regulate transfers and partitions but do not create a statutory bar once the specified conditions are fulfilled.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(2) of the Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans Abolition Act, 1950, and section 7(3) of the Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, impose conditions on transfer and partition; they do not prohibit either absolutely. The Court approved Laxmibai Sadashiv Date v. Ganesh Shankar Date and Dhondi Vithoba Koli v. Mahadeo Dagdu Koli, and overruled Kalgonda Babgonda Patil v. Balgonda Kalgonda Patil.

predicates.land_was_regranted_as_occupancy_land: The land was granted again as occupancy land after the former tenure ended.
predicates.transfer_or_partition_conditions_were_fu: The required prior sanction was obtained and the prescribed payment was made for the proposed transfer or partition.

issues.definition: A regranted occupancy holding may be transferred or partitioned when the required conditions are fulfilled.
